claims.text: Menu is built on sashimi, tempura, and tonkatsu; tempura and tonkatsu are wheat-battered/breaded and fried, with high cross-contamination risk for shared fryers.
Sashimi and seafood bowls are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which is wheat-based; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Kitchen is centered on fish and seafood prepared daily; broths and dishes are dashi/fish based with no documented vegan preparation.
The menu centers on sashimi, torched nodoguro and seafood bowls, which are eaten with Japanese soy sauce (brewed with wheat); no wheat-free soy alternative is documented.
An entirely seafood-based market counter (oysters, sea urchin, scallops, sashimi, nodoguro) with no documented plant-based options; cross-contact with fish is unavoidable here.
The kitchen fries pufferfish and chicken (wheat-flour batter) and grills skewers in a tiny shared counter space, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable.
The signature doteyaki is simmered in Kaga miso and Ono soy sauce, both of which are wheat-fermented and not gluten-free.
Dishes center on meat skewers, doteni (simmered offal) and seafood; even non-meat items share the same simmering and frying station, so no dish can be considered free of animal products.
Sauces and dressings are all made in-house, so staff can describe what goes into a dish if you ask, though no formal allergen handling is documented.

name: 落雁諸江屋 西茶屋菓寮 味和以 (Rakugan Moroeya Nishichaya Karyo Ajiwai)

claims.text: Traditional menu of rakugan, zenzai, kakigori and namagashi is largely rice-, bean- and sugar-based, which often suits plant-based diners, though no allergen labeling is published.

name: ラーメン みなと屋 (Ramen Minatoya)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles and shoyu/miso seasonings are central to every documented bowl; broth uses chicken, fish, and kombu. No gluten-free option is mentioned.
Shoyu and miso chuka soba are core menu items, indicating wheat-containing soy sauce/miso in the seasoning base.
House broth is made from chicken and fish; even vegetable ramen variations are not confirmed to use a plant-only stock.
Traditional Kaga kaiseki here relies on soy sauce and dashi-based seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and the signature jibu-ni is traditionally thickened with wheat flour.
Cooking is centered on fish/bonito dashi and seafood (sea bream, jibu-ni), so plant-only dishes are not part of the documented menu and shared stocks would be used throughout the kitchen.
Kakigori is served with the ice and syrup separate, so guests can control sweetness and see what they are adding.
